own_scenes.place: Londres (Soho, Shepherd’s Bush) y sur de Inglaterra
own_scenes.desc: Hacia 1964-1965 los mods eran el culto juvenil británico más identificable: no la mayoría de adolescentes, sino el subgrupo que marcaba estilos y gastaba el dinero en ropa, discos, scooters y pastillas, con un relevo de modas maníaco («esto pasó de moda hace tres semanas»). Peter Laurie los vio como estaciones emisoras de un solo hombre, la primera generación que vivía conscientemente en un mundo de comunicaciones de masas; Townshend, como un sistema enteramente masculino. Heredaron de los beatniks las pastillas y las sesiones de toda la noche, cambiando el trad por la música negra americana de baile. Las batallas con los rockers de la primavera de 1964 trajeron titulares sobre «pequeños Césares de serrín».

refs.q: By 1964/5, the mods had become a major cult, the most identifiable British youth subculture.
refs.para: By 1964/5, the mods had become a major cult, the most identifiable British youth subculture. They weren’t the majority of teenagers who liked the Beatles and mainstream pop, but rather a subgroup who set the styles and spent the money – on clothes, records, scooters and their accoutrements, and pills. In an era of reasonably low youth unemployment – the figures for early 1966 showed boys and girls under eighteen at around 5 per cent of the total – the turnover of styles was manic and obsessive.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: The outsiders were becoming insiders. The mods had simply taken over the beats’ pill-popping, all-nighter habit
refs.para: The outsiders were becoming insiders. The mods had simply taken over the beats’ pill-popping, all-nighter habit, with contemporary black American dance music instead of trad, while the mix of sexual freedom, drug experimentation and overt anti-Establishment values that had been rehearsed by those early-1960s pioneers had been assumed by the hit-makers of 1965 and early 1966: the Yardbirds, the Who, the Rolling Stones, all of whom were still in their early to mid-twenties.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

similar_scenes.name: British Graffiti: pub-rock y mods
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Gran Bretaña tenía los pubs: el renacimiento nace de los músicos que tocaban rhythm'n'blues y rockabilly en ellos, y el punk les saca de allí. Surge un nuevo cantautor, anclado en las raíces y consciente de lo social: Dave Edmunds, Nick Lowe, Graham Parker, Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello (el «joven airado» de la new wave, quizá sobrevalorado), Tom Robinson, Ian Dury, Wreckless Eric. Dire Straits; el revival mod de los Jam y los Television Personalities; los Soft Boys de Robyn Hitchcock, cimiento del revival psicodélico; Boomtown Rats, Undertones, Bananarama.

podcast.title: Mid-1960s British Youth Cult
podcast.body: Mod fashion originated in mid-1960s Britain as a distinct youth cult, possessing its own unique philosophy and lifestyle, vividly portrayed in the film "Quadrophenia." "This look had its roots in the mid 1960s and Britain. The mods were kind of a youth cult with their own philosophy and lifestyle. If you've ever seen the film Quadrofemia, you'll know exactly what I'm talking about."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin and Culture
podcast.body: Mod, short for "modernist," emerged from a group who preferred modern jazz over trad jazz. By the mid-60s, their primary musical interests shifted to soul and R&B. It was a working-class subculture, concentrated in southeast England, especially London, fueled by newfound comparative affluence in the early 60s, which provided young working-class people with disposable income for fashion, music, and drugs. "Mod stood for modernist, and the mods emerged from the group of people who liked modern jazz rather than trot, but by this point their primary musical interests were in soul and R&B."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: R&B Music and Scooter Culture
podcast.body: Mods were fervent enthusiasts of rhythm and blues (R&B) music, drawing inspiration from artists like James Brown from the US and local bands such as The Who, The Kinks, and Small Faces. Their signature mode of transportation was a heavily accessorized and highly customized Vespa T-S or Lambretta GT200 motor scooter. "The mods loved rhythm and blues, R&B music, people like James Brown from the States and locally the Who and the Kinks in the Small Faces. Their mode of transportation was a heavily accessorized and highly customized Vespat-TS or Lambreta GT200 motor scooter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ready Steady Go! Connection
podcast.body: The mod weekend would begin on Friday with "Ready Steady Go!," whose catchphrase was "The Weekend starts here." The show, while a general pop program, primarily catered to the emerging mod subculture. "And that entire weekend would kick off on Friday, with Ready Steady Go, whose catchphrase was The Weekend starts here."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Regulated Uniform and Attention to Detail
podcast.body: The Mod uniform was meticulously regulated and policed, emphasizing a sharp appearance and rigorous attention to detail. This included ensuring pants were hemmed to the exact right length, with a cuff allowing for pant swing, maintaining no more than a 1-inch gap between the pant leg and the top of the shoe. "And they wore a uniform which was highly regulated and policed. See the duty of the mod was to look sharp and pay attention to detail. For example, it was very important to have your pants hemmed at exactly the right length. And the cuff had to allow for the swing of your pants so there was never more than a 1-inch gap between the end of your pant leg and the top of your shoe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Revival and Enduring Influence
podcast.body: Mod fashion experienced a significant revival in the 1970s, spearheaded by The Jam, and despite the band's eventual demise, Mod culture and fashion re-emerged, albeit in an altered form, during the Britpop era of the mid-1990s. In the 21st century, pockets of Mods continue to thrive globally, proudly carrying on the fashion attitudes of their predecessors, including driving updated versions of their iconic scooters. "There was a mod revival in the 1970s and was led by the jam. ...Mod culture and fashion survived the demise of the jam and rose again in a somewhat altered form during the Brit pop era of the middle 1990s. And here in the 21st century pockets of mods are thriving around the world with all of them carrying on the proud fashion attitudes of their forefathers. Which includes driving updated version of those cool little scooters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Specific Clothing Items
podcast.body: Mod fashion favored slim-fitting suits, Ben Sherman shirts featuring narrow button-down collars, three-button mohair jackets, and parkas often adorned with distinctive Union Jack flags or target symbols. "Mods favored slim-fitting suits featuring Ben Sherman shirts with narrow button-down collars. Jackets were three button mohairs and there were lots of parkas, often featuring union jacks or targets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Style and Music
podcast.body: Mods had a distinct style featuring sharp Italian suits, pop art, op art, and Black American music or British imitations. Music was primarily functional for dancing, and many mods would take amphetamines to dance through entire weekends at clubs to soul and R&B music. "The mods had a very particular sense of style, based around sharp Italian suits, pop art and up art, and black American music or white British imitations of it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
